sections.html:
Farmington is the seat of Davis County, set against the Wasatch foothills with Kaysville to its north and Centerville to its south. Residents numbered 24,531 in the 2020 count. Four in five homes are lived in by their owners, and values are steep, so even a tired house is measured against polished listings down the street, and buyers notice every flaw.

Buyers who tour here tend to mention Station Park, a shopping center with a FrontRunner stop, and Lagoon, the amusement park that fills about 100 acres inside city limits. The city sits between Ogden and Salt Lake City, a short drive from jobs in either direction. The Farmington Trail Committee maintains 146.49 miles of trails, so a house near a trailhead has a selling point worth naming in any conversation.

sections.h2: Snow, floods and the irrigation system
sections.html:
Snowfall averages 48.6 inches a year, so shoppers study the roof and ask about leaks. Flash floods struck Farmington in the 1920s and 1930s and once more in 1984. If your lot sits close to a creek or a canyon mouth, ask an insurance agent whether flood coverage makes sense and be ready to tell a buyer what you learned.

The Farmington Area Pressurized Irrigation District began serving homeowners in July 1978. Check whether your yard is hooked up, because that question comes early in showings.

  • Keep receipts that show when the roof was replaced and what snow or water damage was repaired.
  • Write down how the yard is watered.
  • Hold on to any insurance paperwork for the lot.
  • Photograph the foundation and basement walls after heavy rain so you can show them dry.

The city recognizes two accessory unit types and a third arrangement that carves a detached unit onto a lot of its own. Each single-family home may have one ADU, no more.

  • Internal ADU: built inside or attached to the main house, on a lot of at least 6,000 square feet.
  • Detached ADU: a permanent building on a foundation, on a lot of at least 10,000 square feet.
  • Subordinate single-family dwelling: its own home on its own lot, with subdivision approval.

Somebody must live on site, either in the main house or in the ADU. After a subordinate dwelling is split off, the owner has to occupy it for two years. Every unit needs a full kitchen, a full bathroom and a parking space off the street, in addition to the main home's parking. Tenants must stay 30 days or longer, which rules out nightly rentals.

Turning existing space into an internal ADU needs a building permit, unless that space was approved for living in the first place. An unpapered basement apartment can derail a buyer who needs a mortgage, so dig out whatever permits exist before showing the house.

Davis County sends the bills, and Utah's statewide calendar governs the dates. Payment is due November 30. If the house is your main residence, the 45% exemption means only 55% of market value is taxed.

The Davis County Controller mails valuation notices at the close of July. Appeals must be filed by mid-September. Phone Tax Administration at 801-451-3331 to learn the exact cutoff. The office is in Room 101 at 61 South Main Street.

Appeals go to the Board of Equalization, which is the Davis County Commission. Only the market value is open to challenge, and the tax rate is not. Filing is limited to the owner or an agent with notarized authorization.

Evidence the board accepts:

  • closing papers signed by the title agent,
  • a complete appraisal by a certified appraiser,
  • sales of at least three similar properties near January 1,
  • proof of a factual mistake, like an incorrect square footage.

A lower valuation trims what you pay while the house waits for a buyer, though it will not change the price a buyer offers.

An unpaid bill does not stop a Farmington sale. The title company requests a payoff figure from the county, deducts it from your proceeds and forwards the money at closing. Once a bill turns delinquent the penalty shrinks if you clear it by January 31, so paying sooner costs less.

If you cannot tell what you owe, call Tax Administration and ask for the balance on your parcel. Give that number to the title officer and closing day holds no surprises.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works in Farmington
sections.html:
Selling for cash here is simpler than a financed sale, since nobody at a bank has to approve the house. You tell us about it, we weigh it against neighboring sales, and the decision to accept stays with you.

  1. Send the address and a few basics.
  2. We study the house and recent sales around it.
  3. You take the offer or turn it down.
  4. The title company searches the record and picks a closing date.
  5. The deed is filed and your payment arrives at closing.

Tell the title company early about an unpaid tax bill or an ADU that never got its permit, so each can be settled ahead of recording.

Without a lender, a handful of familiar hurdles vanish: no loan approval to wait for, no appraisal that might come in short, and no repair list a bank insists on before funding. Photos, open houses and weeks of strangers touring the rooms also drop away.

Title work remains. The title company confirms ownership, searches for liens and drafts the closing papers. If a family trust or an estate holds the deed, say so at the outset, since that adds paperwork on the title side.

Several situations show up before many sales here.

  • An older house in or near the Clark Lane Historic District that needs updating.
  • A basement apartment never permitted as an internal ADU.
  • A detached unit the owner would like to sell apart from the main house, which the city handles as a subordinate single-family dwelling.
  • A valuation notice the owner wants to dispute before selling.

Any of these can drag out a regular listing. A direct sale lets you skip staging and repairs and choose your own closing timeline. Mention them at the start and we will price the house with them in mind.

sections.h2: What to gather before you sell
sections.html: Collect the deed, your latest tax notice, permits for additions or a basement unit, roof and repair records, and a note on how the yard is watered. With these in hand the title work moves faster and the first questions from a buyer already have answers.

faqs.q: What county is Farmington, Utah in?
faqs.a: Davis County. Farmington is the county seat, and the county's Tax Administration office is at 61 South Main Street, Room 101.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Farmington?
faqs.a: November 30, the statewide due date. Unpaid taxes become delinquent after that, with a reduced penalty if everything is paid by January 31.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Farmington property value?
faqs.a: File with the Davis County Board of Equalization once the valuation notice arrives at the end of July. The deadline falls in mid-September, so confirm the date with Tax Administration. Only the market value can be appealed.

faqs.q: Can I rent out a Farmington ADU for short stays?
faqs.a: No. ADU rentals must run 30 days or longer, and the owner must live in either the main home or the ADU.

faqs.q: What size lot do I need for a detached ADU in Farmington?
faqs.a: At least 10,000 square feet. An internal ADU needs a lot of at least 6,000 square feet.
